The reason this matters is how sessions are billed. The
, so every request resends the entire conversation —

— as input tokens. By turn fifty, each request carries fifty turns of history, and you'd pay full rate on all of it, every time. The cache changes the maths: tokens the provider has already processed in an identical prefix are billed as cache tokens, often at a tenth of the input rate or less. On a long session, most of what you send is cache tokens, and the bill stays sane.

The cache is fragile in a specific way: it matches exact prefixes. If anything changes earlier in the conversation — the

reorders content, a timestamp updates, a file's representation shifts — the cache misses from that point onward and everything after it is billed at full input rate. Caches also expire after a few minutes of inactivity, so a session resumed after a long pause re-pays its history once. When a session's cost jumps without an obvious cause, compare cache tokens to input tokens in the usage report — a broken cache shows up there first.
